published_figures.source: Lockheed Martin F-35B product card (2023); Lockheed Martin F-35 Fast Facts (April 2020)
published_figures.figure: Pratt & Whitney's F135 Fast Facts (Q4 2021): the F135-PW-600's "Hover Thrust Class 40,650 lbs" - the lift fan's, the roll posts' and the swivelled nozzle's, without afterburner. Measured at sea level, standing, the nozzle down and the throttle at its STOVL top; loaded full so that it stays on the ground. Lockheed's 2015 F-35B card gives "40,500 lb Vertical", and its hover-pit test of 2009 measured 41,100 against a requirement of 40,550: all within a per cent and a bit of this.

Lockheed Martin's release of 18 March 2010 on the first vertical landing: BF-1 "hovered about 150 feet above the airfield for approximately one minute" before letting down. Lifted vertically to 150 ft by the hover control law in calm air, settled, and held a minute more as a 10 kt wind rises across her from the left over ten seconds - so that her roll and yaw are flown as well as her height and pitch; the most her height strays, which this project holds within 10 ft, and the point she rose from within 30 ft. The weight is this project's (the loading above).

Let down from the 150 ft hover above; the sink as the wheels first touch, held under 6 ft/s (360 ft/min), the touchdown criterion this file's touchdown_fpm cites, and the point it rose from within 30 ft. No F-35B vertical landing sink is published.

**Measured, not published.** Lifted to 150 ft at the vertical-landing loading with her fuel burning, and held until she cannot keep her height within 10 ft; the minutes from settling. Her fuel flow follows her engine's core thrust (JSBSim's turbine), not the lift system's.
From 200 KCAS level at 150 ft to a hover there, at her vertical-landing loading, and held 30 s by the hover law; the most height she loses.
The same at her combat loading, 2,220 lb heavier.
The same at her combat loading, 2,220 lb heavier.

The Selected Acquisition Report's STOVL key performance parameter above: a 600 ft short take-off at the requirement's loading, sea level, a tropical day and 10 kt over the deck. Flown as the measured figure below is, the same flight.

**Measured: inside the requirement's 600 ft (its estimate 569)**, which the figure above holds her to. **It does not validate her flaperons' droop**: how far they droop (20 degrees) and their lift are estimates, and without the droop she takes 699.4 ft - so the 600 ft is met on an estimate, not shown by her model. Flown at sea level on a tropical day - 89.8 F, 17.1 C warmer than standard (MIL-STD-210A's tropical atmosphere, 549.5 R at sea level, as Public Domain Aeronautical Software tabulates it) - into 10 kt: converted at idle on the brakes, which droops her flaperons, the nozzle and the fan's thrust 42 degrees from straight aft (the fan's vane box goes no further aft); the brakes off and full STOVL power; at 70 KCAS both swung to 58 degrees and the nose raised to 2 degrees under the attitude her tail strikes at - her airframe's, read from her model's contacts as the departure and the lander read it (21.6 degrees, so 19.6) - on the stabilator and the thrust split, 0.14 of the split's travel a degree short and 8 a radian a second of pitch rate, the gains the fan's share was flown on before the split; the ground from the brakes' release to the wheels leaving it, and she climbs on to 50 ft without touching again or striking her tail. 708.8 ft before her model had the split and the droop; 699.4 with the split and no droop; 591.5 before each flaperon's droop and roll were held to its travel together (from the review of #179). Swept again at these gains on 2026-10-13: 52 degrees at 60 KCAS 685.3 ft, 58 at 60 722.1, 52 at 70 621.5, 64 at 70 573.8, 58 at 75 613.6, 64 at 75 592.3, 70 at 70 touched again; 58 at 70 is kept, as before. The rotation's gains move it most: 0.14 and 4, 490.8; 0.28 and 4, 430.7 - so the gains are the ones it was flown on, not the shortest found.

The product card's "Speed Mach 1.6"; Fast Facts gives Mach 1.6 "with full internal weapons load". No altitude is given; flown level at every 2,000 ft from 30,000 to 50,000 ft at full throttle, the fastest.

The product card's "Range (Internal Fuel) >900 n.mi/1,667 km"; Fast Facts gives the same on the USMC profile. The profile is not published; flown level at 40,000 ft and Mach 0.8, this project's choice, to the last of its fuel with none kept back, so further than a profile with reserves goes. 1,500 nm bounds a model gone wrong.

**Measured, not published.** No flight manual for this aeroplane is public, so there is no handbook stall speed to hold the model to. This is what the model itself does, flown by the same deceleration the published stall speeds are measured by, on 2026-09-23. What it asserts is that the model still does what it did, not that the aeroplane does it. Measured from entry speeds of 160, 200 and 240 knots it varies by 1.13 of a knot, so the number is the model's and not the entry's.

**Measured, not published**, and the speed it leaves the runway at is this figure's reason for being here. No F-35 take-off speed is public. The one the stall gives, 1.15 times it, is 141 knots, and the model cannot fly there on a runway: the stall above was measured at 31 degrees of incidence, with its engine holding up a third of its weight, and no aeroplane is rotated to 31 degrees with its tail on the concrete. Held at the take-off autopilot's ten degrees from 100 knots, on 2026-09-24, it left the runway at 172 knots - its minimum unstick speed at that attitude - and the speed it lifts off at here is 1.1 times that, as FAR 25.107 has a lift-off speed at least 110 per cent of the minimum unstick speed. The ground roll is what this figure's own flight measures to it, and is held so that the model still does what it did.

**Measured, not published.** No flight manual for this aeroplane is public, so there is no handbook rate of climb and no handbook climbing speed. Both are the model's own, taken on 2026-09-23. **The speed is not the one the ninety-five per cent test picked, nor the 1.3-times-the-stall floor under it, but the lowest speed the aeroplane can actually be climbed at.** At 160 knots - 1.3 times its measured stall - it will fly but it will not climb: the autopilot pinned the nose at its fifteen-degree limit, sat at nineteen degrees of alpha and sank at two thousand feet a minute, which is the back of the drag curve. 180 knots still pins the nose and manages 112 ft/min; 190 climbs. 200 is taken because it leaves room - the nose sits at 13.6 degrees of the fifteen it is allowed, and the alpha at 12.
published_figures.plan_speeds: The slowest, 204 kt, is 5 kt over the slowest that held: its approach speed is a flaps-down figure, and flown clean at 194 kt it lost 108 ft round its 5,446 m circle, and below that more; 199 kt held all four ways. The fastest, 360 kt, a fifth over its start speed, held all four ways.
published_figures.glide_speeds: 204 kt, the slowest a route may fly it, went round unstalled.
published_figures.landing_distance: Measured, not published, on 2026-10-13 by `glideslope_cli land f35b` (linux-release): landed by the approach autopilot from a final-approach gate 2 nm out, on a level runway at sea level in calm air, every tank full, she touched 302 m in at 437 ft a minute and stopped 2720 m past the threshold, which she crossed on the 3-degree glidepath aimed 300 m in, at about 50 ft. Written 2 per cent over that, rounded up to 100 ft, for the drift between machines (her flight is not expected to agree to the metre across platforms). Factor 1: the runway the AI used is not a demonstrated minimum but the landing a plan flies, and for the aircraft that publish one it comes out near the factored figure already (the 172P stops 547 m in against her 1,280 ft times 1.43, 558 m; the F-15C 2,252 m against her 4,200 ft times 1.67, 2,138 m), so it is the runway needed as it stands. Searched again 2026-10-13: the product cards and Fast Facts give no landing distance, and none of a shipborne rolling vertical landing is published. She can land vertically, on a pad, but no plan flies her to a hover yet (Phase 10b: no pilot or AI plan flies the F-35B between jet-borne and wing-borne flight): a planned landing is the approach autopilot's rolling one, so that is her need; when a plan can convert her, a pad will do.
